title: City vape count
text: The city council wants to know what share of adults vape right now, by age group, before it votes on a ban next quarter.

traps.cohort-prospective: Follows people for years to measure new cases. The council needs current prevalence next quarter.
traps.case-control: Sampling people by whether they vape destroys any estimate of how common vaping is.

why: 'What share, right now?' is a prevalence question, answered by one well-sampled snapshot. Put the effort into the sampling frame and weighting, not into follow-up.

title: Tattoo rash
text: Five patients at one clinic developed an unusual rash weeks after getting tattoos with the same new ink. Nothing like it has been published.

traps.rct: Deliberately exposing people to a suspected harm is unethical, and premature.
traps.systematic-review: There is nothing yet to synthesize.

why: A careful case series is the fastest way to raise a signal that others can test. Its job is to describe and alert. A case-control study is the logical next step, not the first.

title: Vanishing butterflies
text: Is a migratory butterfly population declining over the decade, and is the decline steady or sudden?

traps.cross-sectional: One snapshot can't show a trend.
traps.field-experiment: Nothing is being manipulated. The question is what is happening, not why.

why: Trends need standardized counts repeated over many years, the backbone of conservation science. Changes in observers, sites or methods over time are the main enemy.

title: Jupiter census
text: What fraction of nearby Sun-like stars host a Jupiter-mass planet?

traps.case-report: One spectacular planetary system tells you nothing about the fraction.
traps.analytical-model: Formation theory can suggest a number, but this asks for an observed frequency.

why: It's a prevalence question in disguise: a defined sample of stars observed with a known detection completeness. Correcting for what the instrument can't see is the whole game.

title: After approval
text: A new diabetes drug was approved after trials in 3,000 people. How often does it cause serious liver injury now that millions use it?

traps.rct: Seeing a 1-in-50,000 harm would need an impossibly large trial. That is exactly why the approval trials missed it.
traps.cross-sectional: Liver injury is an event over time, not a state at one moment.

why: Post-marketing pharmacovigilance (spontaneous reports plus active monitoring of health records) exists because rare harms are invisible in trials. Signals are then confirmed with analytical studies.

title: Smog atlas
text: Before investing in a big study, you want a quick, cheap first look: do countries with more air pollution have higher asthma rates?

traps.cohort-prospective: Years and millions spent on what should be a cheap first look.
traps.rct: You can't assign air pollution.

why: Comparing aggregate data across countries is the cheapest hypothesis generator there is. Just never conclude that polluted individuals get asthma from it: that's the ecological fallacy.

title: Rare cancer, common spray
text: Is a rare childhood cancer (about 1 in 50,000 children) associated with the mother's use of a common pesticide during pregnancy?

traps.cohort-prospective: You'd need to follow millions of pregnancies to collect a handful of cases.
traps.cross-sectional: It can't establish that the exposure came before the cancer.

why: Rare outcome: start from the cases. Draw controls from the population that produced them, and take exposure from records rather than memory, because grieving parents remember differently. A record-linkage cohort works only if registries already capture the pesticide exposure.

title: Clean-room workers
text: A few hundred workers handle a novel solvent at a single chip factory. Is the exposure linked to later kidney disease?

traps.case-control: The exposure is so rare that almost none of the kidney-disease cases in the population will have had it.
traps.ecological: One factory gives no groups to compare.

why: Rare exposure: sample on the exposure. Employment records let you assemble the exposed workforce and an unexposed comparison group (e.g. office staff) and trace their outcomes. Comparing with the general public invites the healthy-worker effect.

title: Snow shovel
text: Does a bout of heavy physical exertion trigger a heart attack within the following hour?

traps.cross-sectional: It can't capture the hour before an event.
traps.cohort-prospective: You'd need hour-by-hour exertion logs from huge numbers of people to catch a few events.

why: Brief exposure, acute effect: compare each patient's exertion in the hour before their heart attack with their own usual exertion. Every stable personal confounder cancels out.

title: Diet and dementia
text: Is a high intake of ultra-processed food in midlife associated with dementia 20 years later?

traps.rct: Nobody sticks to an assigned diet for 20 years.
traps.case-control: People with dementia can't reliably report their diet from two decades ago.

why: Measure diet before anyone has dementia and wait, or (faster) analyse an existing cohort that recorded diet decades ago. Watch for reverse causation: early, pre-clinical dementia changes eating habits.

title: New pill vs. old
text: Does a new blood-pressure drug prevent more strokes than the current standard drug?

traps.cohort-retrospective: Doctors give new drugs to particular kinds of patients. Confounding by indication makes the comparison unreliable.
traps.case-report: Anecdotes can't estimate a comparative effect.

why: A clean causal question about an intervention you can assign, with genuine uncertainty about which is better: randomize. Conceal allocation, blind if you can, analyse by intention to treat.

title: Peer tutoring
text: Does a new peer-tutoring method raise maths scores? Pupils in the same class share notes and talk constantly.

traps.rct: Randomizing pupils within classes lets the method leak to the controls, diluting the effect.

why: When an intervention spreads between individuals, randomize the group (class or school) instead. Then analyse at the right level, because pupils in the same class aren't independent.

title: Soda tax
text: One state introduced a sugary-drinks tax; its similar neighbour didn't. Supermarket sales data exist for both, three years before and after. Did the tax cut consumption?

traps.cross-sectional: Comparing the two states once, after the tax, can't separate the tax from differences that were already there.

why: Compare the change in the taxed state with the change in the untaxed one. The key assumption, parallel trends, can be checked in the years before the tax.

title: Scholarship cutoff
text: Students scoring 70 or more on a national exam receive a scholarship. Does the scholarship make them more likely to graduate from university?

traps.cohort-retrospective: Comparing all recipients with all non-recipients compares stronger students with weaker ones.
traps.cross-sectional: A one-off comparison of graduates and non-graduates can't separate the scholarship from ability.

why: A student who scored 70 and one who scored 69 are nearly identical, except one got the money. The estimate is local to the cutoff. Check that nobody could nudge their score across it.

title: Sepsis alert
text: A hospital switched on an electronic sepsis alert on a known date. Monthly sepsis deaths are available for five years before and two years after. Did the alert help?

traps.cross-sectional: A snapshot can't see a change.
traps.case-report: One dramatic rescue proves nothing about the death rate.

why: Many time points before and after a sharp date separate the alert's effect from the trend that was already under way. Add a control series (another hospital, or a condition the alert can't affect) to rule out coincident changes.

title: Reunification
text: What did German reunification in 1990 do to West Germany's GDP per capita?

traps.rct: Countries can't be randomized to reunify.
traps.cross-sectional: A one-year comparison with other countries ignores differences that existed before 1990.

why: One treated unit, many possible comparisons: build a weighted blend of other OECD countries that tracked West Germany before 1990, then watch where the paths split. Abadie, Diamond & Hainmueller did exactly this.

title: Her migraine
text: A patient has migraines several times a week. Does a new as-needed migraine drug relieve her attacks better than her usual painkiller?

traps.rct: A trial's average effect doesn't tell you whether this one patient responds.
traps.case-report: An uncontrolled before-and-after story is fooled by regression to the mean: she sought help at her worst.

why: Frequent attacks and a fast-acting drug: randomize which drug she takes for each attack (or block of attacks), blind it with identical capsules, and repeat. The answer is about her.

title: Two inhalers
text: Do two inhaler formulations produce the same improvement in lung function in people with stable asthma?

traps.cohort-retrospective: Patients end up on one inhaler or the other for reasons tied to how severe their asthma is.

why: Stable chronic condition, short-acting reversible effect: each person tries both in random order with a washout. Between-person noise vanishes, so far fewer participants are needed.

title: Three knobs
text: Which combination of fertilizer dose, irrigation schedule and seed variety gives the best yield on real farms?

traps.cross-sectional: Farmers who irrigate more also differ in soil, skill and wealth.
traps.case-study: One farm can't separate three factors and their interactions.

why: Cross the three factors in a factorial layout, randomized to plots in blocks across several farms. One season yields main effects and interactions. This is Fisher's original idea.

title: Weld strength
text: Which of six process parameters (current, speed, gas flow…) drive weld strength in the lab, and do any of them interact?

traps.cohort-retrospective: Past production logs confound settings that operators always changed together.

why: A fractional-factorial screening design tests six factors in a few dozen runs and reveals interactions that one-factor-at-a-time testing misses. Randomize the run order to protect against drift. Simulation helps only if a validated process model exists.

title: Checkout button
text: Will a redesigned checkout button increase completed purchases on a site with 2 million visitors a day?

traps.its: Even a long time series can't separate the redesign from concurrent campaigns, when randomizing visitors costs nothing.
traps.interviews-thematic: Users can't reliably predict their own clicking behaviour.

why: Randomize visitors to the old or new button and compare conversion. Fix the sample size and the metric in advance: peeking until it's significant is the classic A/B-test sin.

title: Rat-free islands
text: Does eradicating invasive rats increase seabird nesting success? There are 20 similar islands, and you have permits for 10 eradications.

traps.cross-sectional: Islands that never had rats differ from rat islands in many other ways.
traps.case-report: One island's success story can't be separated from that year's weather.

why: Randomly choose which 10 islands get eradication and measure all 20 before and after (a randomized BACI design). Random allocation stops you from picking the 'easy' islands. Twenty units is few, so plan the power.

title: Triage rollout
text: The ministry has decided that a new emergency triage protocol will be introduced in all 12 regional hospitals over the next year. Does it reduce deaths?

traps.rct: Triage is a hospital-wide process. You can't randomize individual patients within a hospital.

why: Everyone gets it; only the order is open. Randomize the order in which hospitals switch, and every hospital contributes both control and intervention time. Model the background time trend carefully.

title: Ten candidates
text: A new respiratory virus is spreading fast and ten repurposed drugs have been proposed. Which of them, if any, reduce deaths in hospitalized patients? You have months.

traps.case-report: Early case series claiming miracle cures were widespread and misleading.
traps.cohort-retrospective: Sicker patients get experimental drugs. Confounding by indication.

why: One master protocol, one shared control arm; arms are dropped for futility and new ones added. RECOVERY found that dexamethasone saves lives within about 100 days of launch.

title: Older than the trials
text: Do two classes of diabetes drug differ in their effect on kidney failure in adults over 80, a group excluded from the trials? Insurance claims cover 5 million people.

traps.cross-sectional: It can't capture who started which drug, and when.

why: Write the protocol of the trial you'd like to run (eligibility, treatment strategies, time zero, follow-up) and emulate it in the claims data with new users and an active comparator. This designs out immortal-time and prevalent-user bias; what remains is confounding by indication.

title: Does school pay?
text: Does an extra year of schooling raise later earnings? Compulsory-schooling laws let people born early in the year leave school with slightly less education.

traps.cross-sectional: Ability and family background drive both schooling and earnings.

why: Quarter of birth nudges schooling but (arguably) affects earnings only through schooling, which makes it an instrument. Interrogate that 'only through' assumption hard, and check the instrument isn't weak.

title: LDL: cause or marker?
text: Is lifelong higher LDL cholesterol a cause of coronary heart disease, or merely a marker of other risk factors?

traps.cross-sectional: It can't separate cause from marker, or tell which came first.
traps.ecological: Country-level cholesterol averages say nothing about mechanisms in individuals.

why: People inherit LDL-raising or LDL-lowering variants at conception, essentially at random: a natural lifelong trial. Large genetic consortia make it fast. Pleiotropy (genes acting through other paths) is the threat to check. Trials of LDL-lowering drugs answer a shorter-term version.

title: Who crashes next?
text: Using vital signs and lab values from the electronic record, can we flag ICU patients likely to deteriorate in the next six hours?

traps.case-control: Artificially balancing cases and controls distorts the predicted risks (calibration).
traps.rct: Trials test interventions. First you need a model; an RCT of using it comes later.

why: Develop on one period, then validate on a later period and at another hospital. Guard ruthlessly against leakage, e.g. a lab test that was ordered because the doctor already suspected deterioration.

title: Spring flood
text: How much water will flow into a reservoir next spring, given this winter's snowpack and 40 years of records?

traps.case-study: One past flood year can't forecast the next one.

why: Decades of snowpack and inflow records support a statistical forecast; a physically based hydrological simulation is a strong alternative or complement. Judge either one by its skill on years it never saw.

title: Next superconductor
text: Which of 100,000 hypothetical compounds are most likely to superconduct at high temperature, so the lab can synthesize the top 20?

traps.systematic-review: The compounds are hypothetical. There's no literature on them yet.

why: Train a model on known materials to rank the candidates, optionally refine the shortlist with first-principles simulation, then test the top hits. Report performance on genuinely new chemistries, not near-duplicates of the training set.

title: Biomarker add-on
text: Does adding a new blood biomarker to an established heart-attack risk score actually improve prediction?

traps.case-control: Showing that cases have higher levels proves association, not added predictive value.
traps.rct: No intervention is being tested.

why: Association isn't prediction. Compare the model with and without the biomarker on discrimination, calibration and net benefit, in data the model hasn't seen.

title: Range in 2070
text: Where will a mountain plant species be able to live in 2070 under different climate scenarios?

traps.case-study: One population's story can't map a future range.
traps.rct: You can't randomize climates.

why: Species distribution models link today's occurrences to climate, then project them onto scenarios. Mechanistic (physiological) simulations are a valuable cross-check when the future climate falls outside anything in the training data.

title: Rapid strep
text: How accurate is a new 5-minute strep test compared with throat culture, in children who come to clinics with a sore throat?

traps.case-control: Testing obvious culture-proven cases against healthy volunteers inflates accuracy (spectrum bias).
traps.rct: An RCT asks whether using the test improves outcomes. That's a different, later question.

why: Recruit consecutive children with sore throats, do both tests on everyone, and read each test blind to the other. Sensitivity and specificity only mean something in the population where the test will be used.

title: Burnout scale
text: No good questionnaire exists for 'research burnout' among academics. Build one that others can trust.

traps.cross-sectional: A big survey with an untested questionnaire measures… something.
traps.systematic-review: Reviewing studies can't validate a tool that doesn't exist yet.

why: Generate items from theory and interviews, refine them with experts and cognitive testing, then test factor structure, reliability and validity in fresh samples. An exploratory sequential mixed-methods design is essentially this.

title: Two readers
text: Do two radiologists give the same osteoarthritis grade when they read the same knee X-rays?

traps.diagnostic-accuracy: Accuracy needs a reference standard. The question is agreement between readers.
traps.cross-sectional: Grades from different patients read by different radiologists can't measure agreement.

why: Both read the same representative set of images, independently and blind to each other; quantify agreement with weighted kappa. The images must span the full range of severity.

title: Wrist vs. cuff
text: Can a cheap wrist-worn sensor replace the hospital's validated blood-pressure monitor?

traps.ecological: Comparing average readings across clinics hides how far the two devices disagree in each person.
traps.rct: No one needs to be randomized. The question is whether two instruments agree.

why: This is a method-comparison study: measure the same people with both devices and compute Bland–Altman limits of agreement. Decide in advance what difference is clinically acceptable, and don't trust correlation: one device could read 15 mmHg high every time and still correlate perfectly. Include people across the whole blood-pressure range.

title: Lead in the water
text: Fifteen labs measure lead in drinking water using the same standard method. Do they get the same answer from the same sample?

traps.systematic-review: Published results come from different samples and can't isolate lab-to-lab variation.
traps.surveillance: Monitoring tap water over time tells you about the water, not about the labs.

why: Send identical, homogeneous samples (ideally with a certified reference value) to every lab, and quantify repeatability and reproducibility (ISO 5725).

title: Engine limit
text: What is the maximum possible efficiency of ANY heat engine operating between a hot and a cold reservoir?

traps.factorial-doe: Testing engines shows what has been achieved, never what is impossible for every engine.
traps.simulation: It simulates particular engines. A universal bound needs a derivation.

why: 'Any engine' is a universal claim, and only a derivation from the laws of thermodynamics can establish it. Carnot's bound came from reasoning, not measurement.

title: Bridge in a storm
text: How will a long, slender bridge deck respond to wind speeds you can't safely test on the real structure?

traps.case-report: Tacoma Narrows teaches a lot, but one collapse isn't a design check.
traps.cross-sectional: Surveying other bridges doesn't tell you how this one will respond.

why: Coupled fluid–structure simulation lets you push the virtual bridge to failure. Validate the model against wind-tunnel tests of scale models (the 'ok' answer) before trusting the extreme cases.

title: School closures
text: How might closing schools change the peak of a flu pandemic in a city of two million?

traps.rct: Randomizing closures in the middle of a pandemic is rarely feasible, and far too slow.
traps.cross-sectional: A snapshot can't show the dynamics of an epidemic.

why: An agent-based model with households, schools and workplaces lets you play out scenarios. Present results as ranges under varied assumptions, and check them against data from past epidemics.

title: Clock in a cell
text: A three-gene loop in a bacterium seems to oscillate. Is the negative-feedback loop alone enough to cause oscillations, and under what parameter conditions?

traps.cross-sectional: Snapshots of gene expression can't establish sufficiency of a mechanism.
traps.case-control: There are no cases and controls in this question.

why: Write the dynamics as differential equations and analyse their stability; the conditions for oscillation fall out of the mathematics. Simulation explores the parameter space, and the lab then builds and tests the circuit.

title: Neutron-star crash
text: What gravitational-wave signal should detectors expect when two neutron stars merge?

traps.case-report: One observed merger (GW170817) can't supply templates across all masses and spins.
traps.factorial-doe: Neutron stars can't be collided in a lab.

why: The equations are known but have no closed-form solution in this regime, so numerical-relativity simulations produce the waveform templates that detectors search for. Approximate analytical models cover the early inspiral.

title: Price war
text: Two firms compete by setting prices. Under what conditions will they settle at a stable equilibrium instead of an endless price war?

traps.case-study: One price war's story doesn't establish general conditions.
traps.ab-test: Testing prices on customers doesn't reveal the strategic logic between firms.

why: Game theory derives equilibria, and the conditions for them, from stated assumptions. The answer is only as good as those assumptions: state them explicitly and test how robust the result is.

title: Grasp benchmark
text: Your lab has a new robot-grasping algorithm. Is it actually better than the state of the art?

traps.case-report: A cherry-picked demo video isn't evidence.
traps.interviews-thematic: Opinions about the algorithm don't measure grasp success.

why: Same objects, same robot, same metrics and published baselines, plus ablations and repeated trials with confidence intervals. Report the failures, and test beyond the benchmark: sim-to-real gaps are where claims die.

title: A hand for kids
text: Design a low-cost prosthetic hand for children that clinicians and families will actually adopt.

traps.rct: There's nothing to test yet.
traps.systematic-review: Useful background, but it won't build the hand.

why: Iterate: understand the needs, prototype, test with users, refine. Evaluation is built into every cycle, and later the finished device can face a trial.

title: Review workbench
text: Build a tool that guides researchers through a scoping review, and show that it actually helps them.

traps.rct: A large trial of a tool that doesn't exist yet is premature.
traps.case-report: One happy user isn't an evaluation.

why: Build in short cycles with real researchers, and evaluate each version on real tasks: usability, time taken, and completeness of the resulting review. You are not a neutral judge of your own tool, so let others test it.

title: Will they come?
text: Before a costly multi-site trial: can you recruit frail 85-year-olds into a home-exercise programme, keep them in it for 6 months, and measure falls reliably?

traps.rct: Launching the full trial blind risks a very expensive failure to recruit.
traps.systematic-review: Other trials' recruitment rates help, but they won't tell you about your setting.

why: A feasibility study measures recruitment, retention, adherence and data quality against pre-set progression criteria. Resist reporting its effect estimates: it isn't powered for them.

title: Therapy over a bad line
text: Can an app-based talking therapy be delivered in rural clinics with unreliable internet? Will staff use it, and will patients finish it?

traps.rct: Testing effectiveness before you know it can be delivered wastes the trial.
traps.ecological: Country-level internet statistics say nothing about your clinics.

why: Feasibility first: run it in a few clinics, measure uptake, completion and technical failures, and interview staff and patients about what got in the way.

title: Run it again?
text: Forty randomized trials of exercise for depression report conflicting results. What is the overall effect?

traps.rct: A 41st trial adds one more data point to a pile nobody has weighed.
traps.case-study: Examining one trial in depth can't settle a conflict among forty.

why: Search exhaustively, appraise risk of bias, pool with a random-effects model and explore why the trials disagree. Look for missing small negative trials.

title: Plastic in the soil
text: What has been studied about microplastics in farm soils (which methods, which regions, which outcomes), and where are the gaps?

traps.field-experiment: One more experiment doesn't map a field of research.
traps.network-meta: There's no set of competing treatments to rank.

why: This is a mapping question: chart the literature systematically (PRISMA-ScR) without pooling effects. The output is a map of evidence and gaps that tells everyone what to study next.

title: Six pills, few duels
text: Six antidepressants exist, but few trials compare them head to head; most compare each with placebo. Which works best?

traps.rct: A six-arm head-to-head trial would be enormous, and the indirect evidence already exists.
traps.cohort-retrospective: Prescribing patterns are confounded by indication.

why: Combine direct and indirect comparisons in one network to rank the treatments. Check that the trials are similar enough for indirect comparisons to be fair (transitivity).

title: Three weeks
text: A ministry must decide on a school-ventilation policy in three weeks, and asks what the evidence says.

traps.systematic-review: A full systematic review typically takes a year or more. The decision will be made without it.
traps.cluster-rct: A school trial would report long after the deadline.

why: Streamline a systematic review transparently: a narrower question, fewer databases, single screening with verification. Report what you cut, so readers can judge.

title: Vitamin D for everything
text: Dozens of systematic reviews link vitamin D to outcomes from fractures to cancer to depression. What's the overall picture, and how credible is each claim?

traps.rct: One trial can't test dozens of outcomes at once.
traps.case-report: Individual stories can't grade a body of evidence.

why: Review the reviews: grade each claimed association by its size and credibility, and watch for overlapping primary studies being counted twice.

title: Works here, fails there
text: Community health-worker programmes succeed brilliantly in some countries and fail in others. Why, for whom, and in what contexts?

traps.rct: One more trial in one more context won't explain the variation.
traps.ecological: Country-level correlations can't reveal the mechanisms.

why: Realist synthesis asks how context triggers mechanisms that produce outcomes, drawing on trials, process evaluations and qualitative studies alike.

title: The ignored app
text: Night-shift nurses rarely use a new hand-hygiene reminder app, while day-shift nurses do. Nobody knows why.

traps.cross-sectional: A survey needs answer options, and you don't know the reasons yet.
traps.rct: There's no intervention to test until you understand the problem.

why: When you don't know the variables, ask and listen. Sample night and day nurses purposively and interview them until new themes stop emerging.

title: Waste pickers
text: How do informal waste pickers in a megacity organize their daily work, routes and trade?

traps.cross-sectional: Official surveys rarely reach informal workers, and they miss tacit practices.
traps.prediction-model: There's nothing to predict yet, and no data to train on.

why: Practices people don't put into words are best seen by being there: months of participant observation, field notes, trust. Reflect on how your presence changes what you see.

title: The turnaround
text: One factory cut its defect rate by 80% in a year while its sister plants didn't. What happened, and what can others learn?

traps.rct: The change already happened, in one factory.
traps.cross-sectional: A survey of many plants can't reconstruct what happened in this one.

why: Study one bounded case in depth, using documents, data, interviews and observation. Compare it with a sister plant that didn't improve; otherwise you are only studying the survivor.

title: Back to work
text: There is no theory of how people with long COVID decide when (and whether) to return to work.

traps.cohort-prospective: It tells you how many return, not how they decide.
traps.systematic-review: There's too little to synthesize, and the goal is new theory.

why: 'No theory yet' is the signature of grounded theory: iterative interviewing and coding, and theoretical sampling of new cases to test emerging concepts, until a model of the decision process emerges.

title: What should we measure?
text: Trials of therapies for a rare disease all use different endpoints, so none can be compared. Patients and experts disagree on which outcomes matter most.

traps.rct: Another trial would just add another endpoint to the pile.

why: A Delphi process with patients, clinicians and researchers rates candidate outcomes over several anonymous rounds. It's the standard route to a 'core outcome set', usually preceded by a review of the outcomes in use and by patient interviews.

title: The rural gap
text: A national survey shows rural clinics adopt telemedicine at half the urban rate. Policymakers ask why.

traps.cross-sectional: You already have the 'what'. Another survey won't give the 'why'.
traps.rct: There's nothing to randomize until you know the barriers.

why: An explanatory sequential design: use the survey to pick contrasting clinics (high and low adopters), interview staff to explain the numbers, then integrate the two strands.

title: The tangle clip
text: A nurse has invented a clip that stops IV lines from tangling. Before the hospital pays for prototypes and a patent filing: is it actually new?

traps.design-science: Building and testing first risks a year spent reinventing, or infringing, someone else's patent.
traps.systematic-review: There's no effect to pool, and most prior art for a gadget like this sits in patents and product catalogues, not journals.

why: Novelty is judged against everything made public anywhere, in any language: patents, products, catalogues, theses and papers. Search patent databases by classification code as well as by keyword, because patents rarely use everyday words like 'clip'.

title: Roots of a field
text: Research on 'ecosystem services' has grown for thirty years across ecology and economics. Which classic works form its foundations, and which schools of thought do they fall into?

traps.systematic-review: There's no single effect to pool. The question is how the field is structured.
traps.delphi: Experts tend to nominate the classics of their own school. The citation record shows what the whole field builds on.

why: Two works are linked each time a later paper cites both, so clusters of co-cited works are the field's schools of thought, and the works that bridge clusters show where ecology and economics meet. Normalize for how often each work is cited, and remember that a citation isn't an endorsement.

title: Paper flood
text: Thousands of papers on AI for drug discovery appeared in the last two years. What are the active research fronts right now, and how do they group?

traps.co-citation: Papers this new have barely been cited, so almost nothing links them yet. Co-citation would map their foundations, not today's fronts.
traps.systematic-review: There's no focused question or effect to pool, and thousands of papers is far beyond manual appraisal.

why: Papers that cite the same sources are probably working on the same problem, and that link exists the day a paper is published. Down-weight references that nearly everyone cites (here, the classic deep-learning papers), or they glue every paper into one blob. Then name each cluster by reading its core papers.

title: Grit or not?
text: A popular 'grit' scale predicts which students finish their degrees. Critics say it's just conscientiousness under a new name. Does it measure something distinct?

traps.cohort-prospective: Showing that grit predicts graduation proves nothing new: conscientiousness predicts it too.
traps.reliability: A highly reliable scale can reliably measure the wrong thing.

why: Write down the predicted pattern before collecting data: grit should correlate with conscientiousness, but not so highly that they are the same thing, and it should predict outcomes beyond it. Measure both traits by more than one method (self-report, teacher ratings, behaviour), so shared questionnaire habits don't fake the overlap.

title: The blogs know more
text: Teams keep asking when automating their software tests pays off. Practitioners have written hundreds of blog posts, talks and white papers about it, but only a handful of peer-reviewed studies exist. What is known?

traps.systematic-review: Restricted to peer-reviewed studies, you'd throw away most of what is actually known, and there's no effect to pool.
traps.rct: One more experiment adds a single data point; the question is what the field already knows.

why: When practice runs ahead of research, a multivocal review follows Garousi et al. (2019): search academic databases and the grey literature (Google, practitioner sites, conference talks), grade each grey source for authority, method and objectivity, stop by saturation, and report the white and grey evidence side by side.
